reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: A sight-threatening ophthalmic emergency involving suppurative inflammation of the intraocular cavities that requires immediate specialist referral and intervention
Presents with rapidly worsening vision, increasing pain, redness, lid swelling, and often a hypopyon in the anterior chamber
Most commonly occurs after intraocular surgery (especially cataract surgery), intravitreal injection, or penetrating trauma; endogenous cases arise from bloodborne spread of infection
Acute postoperative cases are frequently caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci; more virulent organisms and trauma-related cases (including Bacillus) cause fulminant disease
Loss of the red reflex and vitritis on examination, with a fibrinous anterior chamber reaction, point to intraocular infection
Fungal and endogenous causes should be considered in immunocompromised patients, intravenous drug users, and those with indwelling lines or systemic sepsis
Management centres on urgent vitreous and aqueous sampling with intravitreal antibiotics; vitrectomy is considered in severe cases with very poor vision
A low threshold for suspicion after any intraocular procedure is essential because delay markedly worsens outcome
reference.pathophysiology: Endophthalmitis is infection and severe inflammation of the intraocular contents, involving the aqueous and vitreous. Organisms gain access exogenously through a surgical wound, injection, or penetrating injury, or endogenously by haematogenous seeding from a distant source. Microbial proliferation within the relatively immune-privileged vitreous triggers an intense inflammatory response; bacterial toxins and inflammatory mediators cause rapid retinal necrosis and irreversible photoreceptor damage, which accounts for the poor prognosis when treatment is delayed.
additionalDifferentials: Severe anterior uveitis with hypopyon (e.g. HLA-B27 associated)
Toxic anterior segment syndrome after surgery
Retained lens fragments or postoperative inflammation
additionalInvestigations: Urgent aqueous and vitreous sampling for Gram stain, culture, and PCR before or at the time of intravitreal treatment
B-scan ultrasonography to assess vitreous involvement when the fundus view is obscured
Blood cultures and a search for a systemic source in suspected endogenous disease
Consideration of fungal cultures and specific stains in at-risk patients
redFlags: Rapidly declining vision with pain and hypopyon after intraocular surgery, injection, or trauma demands immediate referral and treatment
Loss of the red reflex and dense vitritis indicating established intraocular infection
Signs of endogenous spread with systemic sepsis or fever
Fulminant progression suggesting a virulent organism such as Bacillus or a fungus
reference.prognosis: Visual outcome depends heavily on the causative organism and the speed of treatment; low-virulence coagulase-negative staphylococcal cases treated promptly can recover useful vision, whereas virulent bacterial, fungal, or trauma-related infection often results in severe, permanent visual loss despite aggressive therapy.
pitfalls: Attributing early postoperative pain and inflammation to routine recovery and delaying referral
Failing to obtain intraocular samples before starting treatment, losing microbiological diagnosis
Overlooking an endogenous source in a febrile, immunocompromised, or drug-using patient
Not considering fungal infection in indolent or treatment-resistant cases
